title: Why One Strand Is Built in Pieces

scenes.tts: Each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and builds one new strand. But the two old strands point opposite ways. How can one fork build both new partners?
scenes.narration: Each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and builds one new strand. But the two old strands point opposite ways. How can one fork build both new partners?
scenes.caption: Each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and builds one new strand. But the two old strands point opposite ways. How can one fork build both new partners?
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's 16:9 colour map without a reset: parental DNA PURPLE, new DNA CYAN, observations GOLD, eliminated states RED, enzyme blocks GREEN, RNA primers YELLOW. Begin with the carried purple-cyan hybrid duplex from the first end card. It opens into a large Y-shaped fork that fills over 60% of the frame height. Purple template arrows point in opposite directions. The question 'How can one fork copy both?' appears above. Mark the whole cartoon 'schematic'. The fork drifts slowly right.
Keep the fork moving slowly right while the title 'Why One Strand Is Built in Pieces' fades in for two seconds. Purple templates continue separating at the fork.

scenes.tts: Keep the first film's colour map. Purple marks parental templates, and cyan marks new DNA. The parental duplex opens into a moving Y-shaped replication fork. Each purple strand must guide a cyan partner, but the two templates run in opposite directions.
scenes.narration: Keep the first film's colour map. Purple marks parental templates, and cyan marks new DNA. The parental duplex opens into a moving Y-shaped replication fork. Each purple strand must guide a cyan partner, but the two templates run in opposite directions.
scenes.caption: Keep the first film's colour map. Purple marks parental templates, and cyan marks new DNA. The parental duplex opens into a moving Y-shaped replication fork. Each purple strand must guide a cyan partner, but the two templates run in opposite directions.
scenes.visual: The title fades. Enlarge the same fork. PURPLE arrowheads travel along the upper and lower templates in opposite directions. Short CYAN starter blocks hover beside both templates but do not yet grow. Labels 'parental template' and 'new DNA' appear once, then shrink to a small legend.

scenes.tts: Every DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide only to a three-prime end. New DNA therefore grows five-prime to three-prime. A copying polymerase also needs that end paired to its template. Replicative polymerases cannot start a chain. Primase must first supply a short paired primer.
scenes.narration: Every DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide only to a 3' end. New DNA therefore grows 5' to 3'. A copying polymerase also needs that end paired to its template. Replicative polymerases cannot start a chain. Primase must first supply a short paired primer.
scenes.caption: Every DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide only to a 3' end. New DNA therefore grows 5' to 3'. A copying polymerase also needs that end paired to its template. Replicative polymerases cannot start a chain. Primase must first supply a short paired primer.
scenes.visual: A large GREEN polymerase block shaped like a clamp closes around a CYAN strand end labelled '3′'. CYAN nucleotide blocks approach; only the block at the labelled end clicks into place. A RED stop marker appears at the opposite end. A YELLOW primer block then settles on bare purple template, supplying a new labelled 3′ end. This is a labelled-block cartoon with no molecular structure.

scenes.tts: The fork moves right, exposing more purple template. Which cyan strand can grow with that fork while its polymerase extends a three-prime end?
scenes.narration: The fork moves right, exposing more purple template. Which cyan strand can grow with that fork while its polymerase extends a 3' end?
scenes.caption: The fork moves right, exposing more purple template. Which cyan strand can grow with that fork while its polymerase extends a 3' end?
scenes.visual: Return the clamp to the full fork. The fork advances right while the upper and lower PURPLE direction arrows remain opposite. Place a labelled 3′ end on each possible CYAN starter. The question 'Which strand can follow the fork?' spans the top. Both starters pulse equally; no answer is highlighted.
Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the moving-right arrow, both labelled 3′ ends and the question. The fork shimmers and template strands drift apart slightly, but neither cyan strand grows.

scenes.tts: On one template, the growing three-prime end faces the fork. Polymerase follows the opening helix and lengthens one continuous leading strand. Its direction of synthesis stays five-prime to three-prime.
scenes.narration: On one template, the growing 3' end faces the fork. Polymerase follows the opening helix and lengthens one continuous leading strand. Its direction of synthesis stays 5' to 3'.
scenes.caption: On one template, the growing 3' end faces the fork. Polymerase follows the opening helix and lengthens one continuous leading strand. Its direction of synthesis stays 5' to 3'.
scenes.visual: Highlight the upper 3′ end in GOLD. The GREEN polymerase clamp follows the fork right as a continuous CYAN strand lengthens behind it. Label the strand 'leading'. Keep the lower starter neutral and unchanged. The growing strand and fork move together.

scenes.tts: On the other template, the usable three-prime end faces away from the fork. Polymerase cannot reverse its chemistry. Primase starts near the fork, then polymerase extends back toward the previous piece. As more template opens, the cycle starts again. These pieces are Okazaki fragments.
scenes.narration: On the other template, the usable 3' end faces away from the fork. Polymerase cannot reverse its chemistry. Primase starts near the fork, then polymerase extends back toward the previous piece. As more template opens, the cycle starts again. These pieces are Okazaki fragments.
scenes.caption: On the other template, the usable 3' end faces away from the fork. Polymerase cannot reverse its chemistry. Primase starts near the fork, then polymerase extends back toward the previous piece. As more template opens, the cycle starts again. These pieces are Okazaki fragments.
scenes.visual: Highlight the lower template. A GREEN primase block places one YELLOW primer near the fork. A GREEN polymerase clamp moves left from that primer while a short CYAN segment grows behind it. The fork moves farther right; the action repeats with a new primer and segment. Label the pieces 'Okazaki fragments'. Never loop DNA or imply that synthesis reverses.

scenes.tts: The pieces must become one strand. In E coli, DNA polymerase one removes each RNA primer while replacing it with DNA. DNA ligase seals the remaining nick. The finished lagging strand is continuous, although it was built discontinuously.
scenes.narration: The pieces must become one strand. In E. coli, DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer while replacing it with DNA. DNA ligase seals the remaining nick. The finished lagging strand is continuous, although it was built discontinuously.
scenes.caption: The pieces must become one strand. In E. coli, DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer while replacing it with DNA. DNA ligase seals the remaining nick. The finished lagging strand is continuous, although it was built discontinuously.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto two lower fragments. A GREEN block labelled 'Pol I' advances through a YELLOW primer; the yellow blocks transform into CYAN blocks. A tiny gap remains. A GREEN 'ligase' block closes the gap with a bright pulse. Pull back as the separate fragments become one continuous cyan strand.

scenes.tts: Several proteins keep the fork moving. DnaB helicase unwinds the parental duplex. Single-strand binding protein holds the templates apart, and gyrase relieves overwinding ahead. DnaG primase places primers. DNA polymerase three, held by its beta clamp, performs most synthesis.
scenes.narration: Several proteins keep the fork moving. DnaB helicase unwinds the parental duplex. Single-strand binding protein holds the templates apart, and gyrase relieves overwinding ahead. DnaG primase places primers. DNA polymerase III, held by its β clamp, performs most synthesis.
scenes.caption: Several proteins keep the fork moving. DnaB helicase unwinds the parental duplex. Single-strand binding protein holds the templates apart, and gyrase relieves overwinding ahead. DnaG primase places primers. DNA polymerase III, held by its β clamp, performs most synthesis.
scenes.visual: Keep the same fork. Add no more than five labelled GREEN blocks in sequence as each acts: 'DnaB' opens the Y, 'SSB' blocks coat exposed purple strands, 'gyrase' rotates a simple overwinding gauge ahead back toward centre, 'DnaG' places a YELLOW primer, and 'Pol III + β clamp' extends CYAN DNA. Earlier labels shrink into a compact job strip rather than accumulating over the fork.

scenes.tts: Eukaryotes keep the same geometry with different parts and many origins. C M G is the helicase. Polymerase alpha primase starts chains. The usual summary assigns most leading synthesis to polymerase epsilon. It assigns most lagging synthesis to polymerase delta on P C N A.
scenes.narration: Eukaryotes keep the same geometry with different parts and many origins. CMG is the helicase. Pol α-primase starts chains. The usual summary assigns most leading synthesis to Pol ε. It assigns most lagging synthesis to Pol δ on PCNA.
scenes.caption: Eukaryotes keep the same geometry with different parts and many origins. CMG is the helicase. Pol α-primase starts chains. The usual summary assigns most leading synthesis to Pol ε. It assigns most lagging synthesis to Pol δ on PCNA.
scenes.visual: The bacterial job strip transforms in place into a eukaryotic strip: 'DnaB' to 'CMG', 'DnaG' to 'Pol α-primase', 'Pol III' to two blocks labelled 'Pol ε' on the leading track and 'Pol δ' on the lagging track, and 'β clamp' to 'PCNA'. Duplicate the fork into several smaller forks across a long purple chromosome bar to show many origins. Add the on-screen qualifier 'usual summary'.

scenes.tts: Names change, but the constraint does not. Every fork needs a way to open DNA, start new chains, extend them, replace starter material, and seal the products. The text compares these jobs and the evidence behind them.
scenes.narration: Names change, but the constraint does not. Every fork needs a way to open DNA, start new chains, extend them, replace starter material, and seal the products. The text compares these jobs and the evidence behind them.
scenes.caption: Names change, but the constraint does not. Every fork needs a way to open DNA, start new chains, extend them, replace starter material, and seal the products. The text compares these jobs and the evidence behind them.
scenes.visual: Keep the carried eukaryotic fork, then transform its labelled blocks into a horizontal job map: 'open', 'start', 'extend', 'replace', 'seal'. A pulse travels along the map while the fork continues moving behind it. The bacterial labels briefly appear above the same jobs and the eukaryotic labels below, without declaring either set interchangeable.

scenes.tts: Polymerases extend a three-prime end, so one strand is built in pieces. Both strands still obey the same chemistry. The enzyme never changes synthesis direction to solve the geometry. This constraint turns opposite templates into different building patterns.
scenes.narration: Polymerases extend a 3' end, so one strand is built in pieces. Both strands still obey the same chemistry. The enzyme never changes synthesis direction to solve the geometry. This constraint turns opposite templates into different building patterns.
scenes.caption: Polymerases extend a 3' end, so one strand is built in pieces. Both strands still obey the same chemistry. The enzyme never changes synthesis direction to solve the geometry. This constraint turns opposite templates into different building patterns.
scenes.visual: Return to the large carried fork. The upper GREEN clamp advances with the fork while one CYAN strand grows continuously. Below, YELLOW primers appear in sequence and separate CYAN fragments grow away from the fork before joining. Large 3′ badges stay on both growing ends. Both patterns run simultaneously for the final sentence.

End card with one line only, in large centred white text: 'Polymerases extend a 3′ end, so one strand is built in pieces.' Behind it, the same fork continues slowly: one cyan strand lengthens continuously and one gains a short fragment. No title, subtitle, logo line or smaller text appears.
